terms.definition: An observable characteristic of an organism, such as flower color, height, or leaf size, produced by its genes, its environment, or both.
terms.function: Traits are the visible or measurable outcomes that let us study how genes and environment shape a living thing.
terms.whereItIs: Every organism has many traits at once — this component uses one pea plant's flower color, leaf size, and seed pod to show four of the underlying concepts.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding traits explains why offspring resemble parents, how inherited conditions are predicted, and how breeders and researchers improve crops and livestock.

terms.definition: The specific pair of alleles an organism carries for a trait, whether or not both alleles are visible in its phenotype.
terms.function: Genotype stores the full genetic instruction for a trait — both the allele that gets expressed and the one that may be silently carried and passed on.
terms.whereItIs: On a chromosome inside the nucleus of every cell; on this model, revealed as the two-bead allele capsule inside the stem when the Cross-section layer is active.
terms.whyItMatters: Genotype is why two organisms with the same phenotype (like PP and Pp purple pea plants) can still produce very different offspring — the hidden allele matters even when it isn't visible.

terms.definition: The observable trait that actually results from a genotype, sometimes further shaped by the environment.
terms.function: Phenotype is the physical, measurable expression of a genotype — the thing you can actually see, touch, or measure.
terms.whereItIs: On this model, the plant's purple flower at the top of the stem.
terms.whyItMatters: Phenotype is what natural selection, breeders, and doctors can actually observe — genotype has to be inferred from it, from breeding results, or from direct genetic testing.

terms.definition: A trait passed from parent to offspring through alleles carried in reproductive cells or, in plants, seeds — distinct from simply being genetic or visible in one organism.
terms.function: Inherited trait names the act of transmission itself: a parent's alleles being copied forward into the next generation, not just the alleles an organism currently holds (genotype) or how they currently show up (phenotype).
terms.whereItIs: On this model, the seed pod hanging from the stem — its seeds carry copies of this plant's alleles into the next generation.
terms.whyItMatters: Distinguishing 'inherited' from 'genetic in this organism' matters because not everything genetic gets passed on in a simple way, and not everything passed on is obviously genetic at first glance — inheritance is specifically about the parent-to-offspring transfer.

terms.definition: A non-genetic factor — such as light, water, temperature, or nutrients — that can change how strongly a genetically coded trait is expressed, without changing the underlying genotype.
terms.function: Environmental influence explains why organisms with identical genotypes can still end up looking or growing differently, depending on the conditions they experience.
terms.whereItIs: On this model, the visible size difference between the fuller leaves on the sun-facing side of the stem and the smaller leaves on the shaded side — both grown from the exact same genotype.
terms.whyItMatters: Environmental influence is why identical twins can look slightly different, why the same crop variety yields differently on different farms, and why genotype alone can't always predict the final phenotype.

terms.definition: A segment of DNA that contains the instructions for a specific trait.
terms.function: Genes are the units of hereditary information — the instructions that, combined with environment, produce an organism's traits.
terms.whereItIs: Located at a specific position along a chromosome inside the cell nucleus.
terms.whyItMatters: Every allele, and therefore every genotype, is a version of a gene — genes are the underlying molecular basis every concept in this component builds on.

terms.definition: One version of a gene; organisms usually inherit two alleles for each gene, one from each parent.
terms.function: Alleles are the specific variants that combine to form a genotype — for pea flower color, P and p are the two alleles of the same gene.
terms.whereItIs: Paired at the same position on matching chromosomes; on this model, the two beads inside the genotype capsule.
terms.whyItMatters: Which two alleles an organism carries, and whether they're the same or different, determines its genotype and therefore constrains its possible phenotype.

terms.definition: A version of a gene whose trait shows up in the phenotype even when only one copy is present.
terms.function: A dominant allele masks a paired recessive allele's trait, so a heterozygous organism (one dominant, one recessive allele) shows the dominant phenotype.
terms.whereItIs: On this model, the P allele for purple flower color — present in both PP and Pp genotypes, both of which produce a purple phenotype.
terms.whyItMatters: Dominant alleles are why an organism's visible phenotype can hide a recessive allele it's still capable of passing on to offspring.

terms.definition: A version of a gene whose trait only shows up in the phenotype when two copies are present, with no dominant allele masking it.
terms.function: A recessive allele's trait is hidden whenever a dominant allele is paired with it, and only becomes visible in a homozygous recessive genotype.
terms.whereItIs: On this model, the p allele for white flower color — only produces a white phenotype in the pp genotype.
terms.whyItMatters: Recessive alleles explain why traits can seem to 'skip a generation': they're carried silently by parents whose own phenotype shows the dominant trait instead.
